title: Discharge at the port of destination
sceneDesc: The ship arrives at the destination quay. A quay crane lifts the container off the ship onto a terminal truck, which takes it to the import yard.

narration.1: Welcome to {pod}! My ship berths at {podTerminal}.
narration.2: {vessel} berths at {podTerminal}. The discharge list tells the terminal which boxes come off here. [TO VERIFY:v61]
narration.3: Discharge planning from the BAPLIE and import manifest; customs has risk-assessed the cargo data, and some boxes may already be flagged for inspection. [TO VERIFY:v67]

narration.1: A crane lifts me off the ship and puts me down on a terminal truck.
narration.2: Discharge by quay crane; lashings removed first. Damage found at discharge is recorded — key for claims. [TO VERIFY:v62]
narration.3: Discharge and damage survey; seal checked against the manifest. A seal discrepancy here triggers investigation and possibly a customs hold.

1.reefer: I'm taken to the import yard and plugged in again. The customer has been told I've arrived.
1.*: I'm taken to the import [[yard]] to wait for my paperwork. The customer has been told I've arrived.

narration.2: Import yard. The [[arrival-notice]] went to the consignee and notify party: charges due, free time and release conditions. The [[demurrage]] free time starts at discharge. [TO VERIFY:v66]
narration.3: Import dwell: demurrage/storage free time running; customs selection (scan, physical) adds moves and days. Combined D&D tariffs may apply. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v66]
Customs selects the box for a scan and physical inspection: 3 extra days. Demurrage free time ends tomorrow. The consignee asks the carrier to waive all demurrage 'because it's customs' fault'.

GYE-ANR.1: Antwerp-Bruges is one of Europe's largest container ports, and a major hub for fruit. [TO VERIFY:v74]
GYE-ANR.2: Antwerp-Bruges handles around 13 million TEU a year. [TO VERIFY:v74]

*.1: Le Havre is France's largest container port. [TO VERIFY:v74]
*.2: HAROPA (Le Havre, Rouen, Paris) handles around 3 million TEU a year, most of it at Le Havre. [TO VERIFY:v74]

body.1: The crane lifts me off the ship. Workers check that I'm not damaged and that my seal is intact.
body.2: Discharge sequence follows the bay plan; damage and seal checks are recorded. [TO VERIFY:v62]

body.1: A message from the carrier to the customer: 'Your container has arrived. Here is what you need to pay and do to collect it.'

body.2: Import [[demurrage]] runs from discharge (or day after) until full gate-out, after the free time. Illustrative: {freeDays} days free, then {cur}40/day storage-type charges. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v12]
body.3: Customs inspections, missing originals or unpaid freight don't stop the clock unless the tariff or contract says so. [TO VERIFY:v72]

body.1: {importCustoms} check the data about me. Most containers are not opened.
body.2: Risk analysis on ENS and declarations; selected boxes are scanned or inspected, with moves and costs for the cargo side. [TO VERIFY:v67]

body.1: Back on electricity so {cargo} stays at {setPoint}.
body.2: Reefer plugged in the import rack; plug-in and monitoring charges may apply after free time. [TO VERIFY:v57]

1.2: Collect freight and destination charges must be paid (or covered by credit) before release. Charge names and amounts vary by carrier and port. [TO VERIFY:v35] [TO VERIFY:v66]

2.2: Free time per tariff or contract; after it, daily charges apply. [TO VERIFY:v21]

3.2: Carrier release (commercial) and customs release (legal) are two different things — both are needed. [TO VERIFY:v68]

2.prompt: What does the consignee need to obtain release from the carrier?

options.text: An original B/L (or waybill / express release) and the charges paid

options.fb: The VGM matters for loading at origin, not for release.
The booking is the shipper's contract document at origin.

2.explain: Carrier release depends on the transport document and payment; customs release is needed in addition. [TO VERIFY:v68]

3.prompt: Freight is collect. The consignee pays destination THC but disputes the ocean freight amount. Can the carrier release?

options.text: Not until the collect freight is paid or covered by an agreed credit/guarantee — the dispute is handled separately
Yes, THC is the only charge needed for release
options.fb: Collect freight is part of what must be settled.

options.text: Yes, if the original B/L is presented
options.fb: The B/L is necessary but not sufficient when freight is collect.
Payment conditions are a carrier matter.

3.explain: Carriers usually hold cargo until collect freight is paid (lien rights depend on the B/L terms and law); disputes go to sales/credit. [TO VERIFY:v33]

documents: **Arrival notice** — charges, free time, release conditions. [TO VERIFY:v66]
costs: **Collect freight** when freight terms are collect.
**Inspection costs** if customs selects the box. [TO VERIFY:v67]
risks: **Damage found at discharge** → survey and claims.
**Consignee not reachable** → box sits, demurrage builds.
jobs: **Import customer service** — arrival notices, release questions.
**D&D team** — demurrage invoicing and disputes. [TO VERIFY:v72]

incoNote.C: Under C-rules, the seller's costs end here at the destination port; destination charges depend on the contract of carriage.
incoNote.D: Under D-rules, the seller still carries the risk and organises the next steps; import clearance is the buyer's (DAP/DPU) or the seller's (DDP).
incoNote.*: Under {incoterm}, the buyer has carried the risk since step {riskStep}.

1: At {pod}, a crane unloads me and I wait in the import yard.
The carrier sends an arrival notice to the customer.
A free-time clock starts: waiting too long costs money.
2: Discharge checks (damage, seal) are evidence for claims.
The arrival notice sets charges, free time and release conditions.
Import demurrage runs from discharge until gate-out, after free time.
3: Customs inspections don't stop demurrage by default — check the tariff and contract.
Collect freight must be settled before release.
Waivers are commercial decisions, documented and approved.

1.prompt: I'm in the import yard. What happens next?
1.hint: Two organisations must say 'yes' before I can leave the port.

options.text: Customs clears me, and the carrier releases me to the customer.
options.confirm: Exactly. Customs gives the legal green light; the carrier gives the commercial one (paperwork and payment). Under {incoterm}, import customs is the {importBy}'s job.

options.text: A truck takes me straight to the customer.
options.why: I can't leave the terminal without customs and carrier release.
options.realLife: The gate would refuse the truck.

options.text: I go back to sea to the next port.
options.realLife: Taking me back would cost a lot and delay the customer.
options.whenRight: Only if I was discharged by mistake.

2.prompt: Box discharged at {pod}, arrival notice sent. What happens next?

options.text: Import clearance by the consignee's broker; B/L surrender and charges paid to the carrier; carrier and customs releases sent to the terminal.
options.confirm: Correct. Two releases are needed: customs (legal) and carrier (commercial). Under {incoterm}, import clearance: {importBy}. [TO VERIFY:v67] [TO VERIFY:v68]

options.text: The terminal releases the box on presentation of the arrival notice.
options.why: The arrival notice is information, not a release.
options.realLife: Terminals only release against carrier and customs releases.

options.text: With freight prepaid, the box is released without any document.
options.why: Prepaid freight doesn't replace the B/L, waybill or express release.
options.realLife: Releasing without the right document risks misdelivery.
options.whenRight: With a sea waybill or express release, no original is needed — but release is still controlled. [TO VERIFY:v68]

options.text: The shipper presents the export declaration at {pod}.
options.why: Export clearance was done at origin.
options.realLife: Destination customs need the import declaration.

3.prompt: Case: customs inspection adds 3 days; free time ends tomorrow; the consignee asks for a full demurrage waiver. What is the correct response?

options.text: Explain that demurrage runs per tariff/contract, inspections included unless agreed otherwise; give the daily rate; help speed up clearance; refer any goodwill waiver to the commercial owner.
options.confirm: Right. Customs delays are normally for cargo account; consistent application of the tariff and documented exceptions avoid disputes. Some regulators set billing rules. [TO VERIFY:v72]

options.text: Waive everything: customs delays are never the customer's fault.
options.why: Waivers outside the tariff create inconsistency and revenue leakage.
options.realLife: Other customers will ask for the same.
options.whenRight: If the contract has a customs-inspection clause.

options.text: Stop the clock until customs finishes.
options.why: Clock events are defined by the tariff, not by the situation.
options.realLife: An unauthorised stop is a billing error.
options.whenRight: If the tariff explicitly suspends free time for inspections.

options.text: Tell the consignee to ask customs to pay.
options.realLife: Unhelpful and damaging to the relationship.
